questions.text: The Planck statement of the Third Law says that:

options.label: a
options.text: Absolute zero can be reached in one step

options.label: c
options.text: Heat capacity becomes infinite at 0 K

options.label: d
options.text: The entropy of a perfect crystalline substance approaches zero as $T\rightarrow0\ \mathrm{K}$

questions.detailed: At absolute zero a perfect crystal has a single equilibrium microstate, so $S\rightarrow0$. This gives a physical zero for entropy, which is why absolute entropies can be tabulated.

questions.text: The unattainability statement of the Third Law states:

options.label: a
options.text: Absolute zero is easily reached with modern technology

options.label: b
options.text: It is impossible to reach $0\ \mathrm{K}$ by any finite sequence of processes — temperatures arbitrarily close may be approached

options.label: c
options.text: Entropy is zero at all temperatures

options.label: d
options.text: Heat capacities vanish at room temperature

questions.detailed: No finite number of operations can reach exactly $0\ \mathrm{K}$; each cooling step removes a smaller fraction of the remaining energy. $T\to0$ is approached asymptotically.

questions.text: "The absolute entropy of an element can be taken as zero at 298 K."
questions.detailed: False — and this is the single biggest entropy trap. Elements have zero *enthalpy of formation*, but their *absolute entropy* at 298 K is positive (from the Third Law). Only at 0 K does a perfect crystal have $S=0$.

questions.text: Given $S^\circ_{300}(\mathrm{Cu})=8.0\ \mathrm{cal\,deg^{-1}mol^{-1}}$ and $C_P(\mathrm{Cu})=5.41+1.50\times10^{-3}T$, the standard entropy of solid copper at $1346\ \mathrm{K}$ is:

Zinc melts at $693\ \mathrm{K}$ with $\Delta H_{\text{fus}}=1740\ \mathrm{cal\,mol^{-1}}$. Given $S^\circ_{298}=9.95$, $C_P(\text{solid})=5.35+2.40\times10^{-3}T$ and $C_P(\text{liquid})=7.50\ \mathrm{cal\,deg^{-1}mol^{-1}}$, $S^\circ$ of liquid Zn at $1023\ \mathrm{K}$ is about:
Which of the following would retain non-zero entropy at 0 K?

options.label: a
options.text: A perfect crystal of CO with frozen, randomly oriented molecules

options.label: b
options.text: A perfect single crystal of a pure metal

questions.detailed: Solid CO can freeze with its molecules in random orientations (two orientations each), giving a *residual entropy* $S_0\approx R\ln2$ even at 0 K. The Third Law applies strictly only to a perfect (unique-configuration) crystal, which is why the others do reach $S=0$.

questions.text: Why must the Third Law be invoked to obtain *absolute* entropies from calorimetry?

options.label: a
options.text: Because entropy is a state function

options.label: b
options.text: Because it fixes the otherwise-unknown integration constant: $S=0$ at $0\ \mathrm{K}$ for a perfect crystal, so $S_T=\int_0^T (C_P/T)\,dT$

options.label: c
options.text: Because heat capacity is zero everywhere

options.label: d
options.text: Because enthalpy needs a reference too

questions.detailed: Entropy is defined only up to an additive constant in classical thermodynamics. The Third Law supplies that constant ($S\to0$ as $T\to0$ for a perfect crystal), making $S_T=\int_0^T(C_P/T)\,dT$ absolute.

statements.text: At $0\ \mathrm{K}$ the heat capacity of a solid tends to zero.
Absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
Absolute entropies allow $\Delta S^\circ$ of a reaction to be computed from tables without needing any entropy reference reaction.

questions.detailed: All three are true. $C_P\to0$ as $T\to0$ (I), absolute zero is unattainable in finite steps (II), and because Third-Law entropies are absolute, reaction $\Delta S^\circ$ follows directly from $\sum S^\circ_{\text{prod}}-\sum S^\circ_{\text{react}}$ (III).

questions.assertion: Absolute zero of temperature is unattainable.
questions.reason: As $T\rightarrow0$, the entropy of a perfect crystal tends to zero, so no finite cooling process can drive it further.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: As $T\to0$ the isothermal entropy change for any reversible step also tends to zero, so the efficiency of cooling collapses and infinitely many steps would be needed to reach $0\ \mathrm{K}$. The vanishing-entropy behaviour (R) is why absolute zero is unattainable (A).

questions.text: "For a perfect crystal, entropy is zero at $T=0\ \mathrm{K}$ even if the substance is a compound rather than an element."
questions.detailed: True. The Third Law is about a *perfect crystal* of any substance (compound included) having a unique microstate at 0 K, so $S=0$. It is not restricted to elements.

questions.text: A reaction has $\Delta S^\circ=[2(50)+3(200)]-[80+3(5)]\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Its value is:
questions.detailed: Products: $2(50)+3(200)=100+600=700$. Reactants: $80+15=95$. $\Delta S^\circ=700-95=+685\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Note every species — elements included — carries its real $S^\circ$ (no zeros).

questions.text: The Nernst heat theorem is closely associated with which law?
questions.detailed: Nernst's heat theorem (that $\Delta S\rightarrow0$ for condensed-phase reactions as $T\rightarrow0$) is the historical foundation of the Third Law and the basis of absolute entropy tables.

questions.text: As temperature approaches absolute zero, the heat capacity $C_P$ of a solid:
questions.detailed: $C_P\to0$ as $T\to0$ (a consequence of quantised lattice vibrations). This is essential for the integral $\int_0^T(C_P/T)\,dT$ to remain finite.

questions.text: Using absolute entropies, $\Delta S^\circ_{298}$ for $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3+3C\rightarrow 2Cr+3CO}$ with $S^\circ(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3})=81.17$, $S^\circ(\mathrm{C})=5.69$, $S^\circ(\mathrm{Cr})=23.76$, $S^\circ(\mathrm{CO})=197.90\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}mol^{-1}}$ is about:
questions.detailed: $\Delta S^\circ=[2(23.76)+3(197.90)]-[81.17+3(5.69)]=[47.52+593.70]-[81.17+17.07]=641.22-98.24\approx+543\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Strongly positive because 3 mol of gas (CO) are generated from all-solid reactants — a large entropy gain.
